contexts.text:
Which problem comes first?

At an imaginary workshop, one computer could not display the instructions. A second problem was that the printed cover had the wrong colour. The group described the display problem as urgent because it stopped the activity. The colour issue was minor and could wait.

They raised both problems with the organizer, who addressed the display issue first. A loose connection was found and the instructions became visible. The group then returned to the cover. Separating importance from urgency helped them discuss the problems without exaggerating either one or pretending that neither existed.

Building an argument

In a fictional writing class, Leila outlined an argument before drafting her essay. Her first paragraph stated a position. The next paragraphs explored the reasons, illustrated them with examples and acknowledged a limitation. The conclusion returned to the original question.

During review, she found one assertion that was stronger than her evidence supported. She qualified it rather than hiding the uncertainty. Her partner also noticed an example that did not relate to the argument, so she removed it. The final essay was shorter, but its ideas were more coherent and its stance was easier to follow.

One phrase, several meanings

These are fictional office notes. At nine, Amir tried calling the supplier but could not get through. At ten, he set up a meeting for the afternoon. Before lunch, he went through the order details carefully. At two, a colleague took over from him while he attended a class.

The notes use familiar phrasal verbs in different ways. Getting through concerns telephone contact here. Setting up concerns arranging an event, and going through concerns checking information. Taking over means assuming another person’s responsibility. The surrounding words make the intended senses clear.

Briefly and simply

At a fictional training session, Jo said, “I briefly worked in the archive.” Here, briefly described a short period of time. Later she said, “I will briefly explain the filing system.” In that sentence, briefly meant using few words.

The trainer added another contrast. A rule could be strictly applied, meaning that no exceptions were allowed under that rule. A statement could also be “not strictly true,” meaning not completely exact. The learners wrote their own examples, using context to identify the sense rather than assuming that each adverb had only one meaning.
